scenario: AITA for Seeking Prayers at a Scheduled Prayer Service? | Hello all. This week I was at a prayer service at my college fellowship. We have these once a week, and they are open to the public. A student at our school died recently in an accident, and so there were more people at the service than normal. Lots of people were crying. I did not know him, but I still prayed for him with everyone else. During the service, people offer up statements and some ask for prayers. This time, lots of people were remembering the student but a few people asked for prayers for sick relatives, one for her cousin who was struggling with drug addiction, and then it came to me. I broke up with my girlfriend of about 3 months two weeks ago, and it has been really tough on me. She was also at the prayer service even though she is not as Christian as I am and normally was not there. She just happened to know the student who passed away. I asked people to pray for me that I recover from my breakup and that in the future I only date people who truly share my religious values because those people would not be hurtful. Fast forward to that afternoon, I got messages from several of my friends telling me that asking for prayers, during a prayer service, was inconsiderate. My ex girlfriend also sent me a message telling me that she found it hurtful and that she would prefer that I not speak about her again, at least not when she is present. I asked her what was wrong with what I said, and she told me I was attacking her. I was not! I never attacked her. I understand that people there were suffering, but we all suffer for different reasons. I am also suffering. I have never had such a tragic breakup, and I thought she was the one who I would marry. I was already looking at rings, and then she just broke up with me. I have a right to be sad, don't I? I have a right to ask to be lifted in spirit--we all have different crosses to bear. A couple of my friends are not even talking to me. Am I really wrong here? I am interested in what you have to say.

Informal groups may lack these structures, offering more flexibility but potentially less consistency in encouragement and accountability. 3. **Sense of Community:** - Both settings provide a sense of belonging, which is crucial for motivation. Religious communities may have a stronger sense of unity due to shared rituals and traditions, while informal groups rely on mutual respect and shared experiences. 4. **Leadership and Mentorship:** - Religious communities often have formal leaders who provide guidance. Informal groups may have informal leaders, offering a different kind of support but potentially less consistent mentorship. 5. **Accountability and Support:** - Both settings offer support, though religious communities may have more structured systems. Informal groups rely on mutual encouragement, which can be effective but may vary in consistency. 6. **Personal Reflection and Growth:** - Religious communities often emphasize practices like prayer or meditation. Informal groups may focus on discussion and personal reflection, offering a different approach to self-improvement. 7. **Community Service and Giving:** - Both settings value service, though religious communities may have more structured opportunities. Informal groups may encourage kindness and helping others in a more flexible manner. 8. **Long-term Commitment and Shared Experiences:** - Religious communities often have a long-term perspective, while informal groups may have more flexible commitments. Shared experiences in both settings can build trust and camaraderie. ### Conclusion: While informal groups lack the formal structures of religious communities, they can still significantly encourage personal growth through shared values, mutual respect, and support. The informality allows for flexibility and personalization, which can be advantageous for some individuals. However, the absence of structured accountability and consistent practices may be a limitation. Despite these differences, the strength of relationships and commitment to shared values can create a supportive environment that motivates and encourages personal development. Thus, the influence of such a group can be as effective as that of a religious community, depending on the individuals involved and their commitment to growth.
